title: Objects, Functions, and Classes
summary: Functions, this, objects, prototypes, classes, modules and closures: how JavaScript code is shaped and how it runs.

lessons.title: Declarations, expressions and arrows
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, locate the best function implementation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **function** is a named set of steps you can run again and again. You run ("call") it with parentheses, like `add(2, 3)`. JavaScript gives you three ways to write one: a **function declaration**, a **function expression** and an **arrow function**. They differ in when you can call them and in a few hidden extras.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Three ways to put a recipe on the kitchen wall. A declaration is pinned up before cooking starts, so you can use it any time. An expression is pinned only when you reach that step. An arrow is a short note, pinned just as late. Where it stops: arrows also lack some extras, shown below.

cards.title: Three ways to write it
cards.code:
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }          // declaration
const sub = function (a, b) { return a - b; }; // expression
const mul = (a, b) => a * b;                   // arrow
cards.body: All three take `a` and `b` and give back one value. `=>` points from the inputs to the result, so `mul(2, 3)` gives `6`. With no curly braces, an arrow returns its one expression by itself. That is an **implicit return**. Add braces and you need `return` again.

cards.title: Declarations are ready early
cards.body: **Hoisting** means JavaScript sets up declarations before it runs any line. A function declaration is set up with its whole body. So you can call `add(2, 3)` on a line above `function add`, and it still gives `5`.

cards.title: Expressions wait for their line
cards.body: A function expression lives in a variable: a named box made with `var`, `let` or `const`. The box is empty until its line runs. A `var` starts as `undefined`, and calling `undefined` throws `TypeError`. A `let` or `const` name is locked until its line, so an early call throws `ReferenceError`.

cards.title: What arrows don't have
items: No own `this` (the object a function works for). An arrow uses the `this` of the code around it
No own `arguments` (a list of all values passed in)
Can't be used with `new`, the keyword that builds objects: it throws `TypeError`
So it's a poor fit for an object **method**: a function stored on an object, like `cart.total()`

cards.title: Returning an object from an arrow
cards.code:
const bad = () => { id: 1 };    // returns undefined
const good = () => ({ id: 1 }); // returns { id: 1 }
cards.body: `bad()` gives `undefined`, because its braces are read as a function body, not an object. `good()` gives `{ id: 1 }`. So wrap the object in parentheses.
"An arrow is just a shorter function." Not quite. Use an arrow as an object method and `this` is not the object. It is whatever `this` was outside. And `new` on an arrow throws `TypeError`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Declarations rise, expressions wait, arrows borrow."** Declarations are hoisted with their body. Expressions wait for their line. Arrows borrow `this`.

The word that ends a function and hands a value back. A function with return 5 gives back 5.

The oldest way to make a variable. It is set up early and holds undefined until its line runs.
Makes a variable you can give a new value later. The name is locked until its line runs.
Makes a variable you can't point at a new value later. The name is locked until its line runs.
The value a variable has when nothing has been put in it yet.
The error you get when a value is the wrong kind for what you do, like calling something that is not a function.
The error you get when you use a variable name that doesn't exist yet, or isn't ready to use yet.
A hidden value inside a regular function. It points at the object the function is working for, like cart in cart.total().
A list-like object that regular functions get. It holds every value passed in. Arrow functions don't get their own.

lessons.title: Defaults, rest, spread and arguments
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, locate the best function implementation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Parameters** are the named slots in a function's definition. **Arguments** are the real values you pass in when you call it. In `greet('Ann')`, `'Ann'` is an argument. JavaScript is relaxed about the count. Pass fewer and the missing ones are `undefined`. Pass more and the extras are ignored, unless you collect them.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A lunch order form. Each box is a parameter. A **default** is a box pre-filled with "water" if you leave it blank. A rest parameter is the line "anything else" that gathers all extras into one list. Where it stops: writing "null" in a box counts as filled, so the default is not used.

cards.title: Default parameters
cards.body: A **default parameter** is a backup value written with `=`. It is used only when the value is `undefined`, given or missing. So the first two calls give `'Hi friend'`. `null` is a real value, so `greet(null)` gives `'Hi null'`. The same goes for `0` and `''`.

cards.title: Rest parameters
cards.body: A **rest parameter** (three dots before the last name) gathers the leftover values into a real array. Here `nums` is `[1, 2, 3]`. Then `reduce()` adds them up, so the call gives `'Sum: 6'`. Rest must be the last parameter, and only one is allowed.

cards.title: Spread is the reverse
cards.body: **Spread syntax** uses the same three dots to unpack. `Math.max()` gives the biggest number you pass it. `Math.max(...[3, 9, 4])` passes 3, 9 and 4 as separate values, so it gives `9`. In an **array literal**, `[...a, ...b]` joins two arrays. `{ ...obj }` copies an object's properties.

cards.title: The old arguments object
cards.body: Regular functions also get `arguments`. It is an **array-like** object holding every value passed in. It has `length` (how many values) and numbered slots, like `arguments[0]`. But it has no array methods, such as `map()`. Arrow functions don't have their own. In new code, prefer a rest parameter.
"`null` triggers the default." It doesn't. Only `undefined`, passed or missing, uses the default. Also, rest must come last: `function f(...a, b)` is a `SyntaxError`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Rest packs, spread unpacks."** Three dots in a parameter list gather. Three dots in a call or a literal scatter.

A real value you pass in when you call a function. Regular functions can also see them all in the arguments object.
A backup value for a parameter. It is used only when the value passed in is undefined or missing.
A last parameter written with three dots. It collects all the leftover values into a real array.
Three dots that unpack an array or object into separate values, for a call or a new array or object.
An array written straight out in square brackets, like [1, 2, 3].
Something with a length and numbered slots, like an array, but without array methods such as map or filter.
The value a variable or parameter has when nothing was given to it.
A value that means "empty, on purpose". It counts as a real value, so it doesn't use the default.
Walks through an array and folds all its items into one value, like adding them up. [1, 2, 3] can become 6.
Gives back the biggest of the numbers you pass in. Math.max(3, 9, 4) gives 9.
How many items something holds. A list of three values has length 3.

The error for code that isn't written correctly. JavaScript finds it while reading the code, before running it.

lessons.title: Higher-order functions and callbacks
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, locate the best function implementation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: In JavaScript, functions are **first-class**: they are values, like numbers. You can store one in a variable, pass it to another function, or return it. A function that takes or returns a function is a **higher-order function**. The function you pass in is a **callback**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A delivery app. You hand the driver a note: "when you arrive, ring twice." The note is the callback. The driver decides when to use it. Where it stops: some callbacks run right away, like the one you give `map()`. Others run later, like the one you give `setTimeout()`.

cards.title: map and filter take callbacks
cards.body: `map()` calls your callback once per item and builds a new array from the answers. `filter()` keeps only the items where your callback returns `true`. Neither one changes `prices`.

cards.title: reduce folds a list into one value
cards.code:
const prices = [10, 25, 40];
const sum = prices.reduce((acc, p) => acc + p, 0); // 75
cards.body: `reduce()` also calls your callback once per item. `acc` is the running total, and it starts at `0`, the last value you pass. Each round returns `acc + p`, which becomes the next `acc`: 10, then 35, then `75`.

cards.title: Functions that return functions
cards.body: A **factory function** returns a new function. `multiplier(2)` returns an arrow that multiplies by 2, so `double(5)` gives `10`. `double` still knows `factor` after `multiplier` has finished. Calling in a chain, like `add(1)(2)`, is called **currying**.

cards.title: Pass it, don't call it
cards.body: Pass `save`, not `save()`. The parentheses run it now and pass its **return value** instead. `setTimeout()` calls a function after a delay in milliseconds. So `setTimeout(save, 1000)` runs `save` one second later. `setTimeout(save(), 1000)` runs it at once.

cards.title: Pure callbacks
cards.body: A **pure function** gives the same output for the same input. It changes nothing outside itself, so it has no **side effects**. Array callbacks should be pure. Then `map` and `filter` stay easy to test.

`['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)` gives `[1, NaN, NaN]`. `NaN` means "not a number". `parseInt()` turns text into a whole number. Its second value is the **radix** (number base). But `map` passes the item, its index and the array. So the index becomes the radix. Use `map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))` or `map(Number)`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Hand over the recipe, not the cake."** Pass the function itself. Adding `()` bakes the cake right now.

terms.say: Functions are plain values in JavaScript. You can store them, pass them around and return them, just like numbers.
A function that takes another function as a value, or returns one. map and filter are examples.
A function you hand to another function, so that function can call it for you, now or later.
Makes a new array by running your function on each item. [10, 25] doubled becomes [20, 50]. The old array stays the same.
Makes a new array with only the items your function says yes to. Keeping numbers under 30 from [10, 40] gives [10].
Walks through an array and folds all items into one value, like a running total. [10, 25, 40] added up gives 75.
Runs a function later, after a wait in milliseconds. 1000 milliseconds is one second.
A function that builds and returns something new each time, like a fresh function or object.
Splitting a function of many values into a chain of one-value functions, called like add(1)(2).
What a function hands back when it finishes. Without a return statement it is undefined.
A function that always gives the same answer for the same input and changes nothing else.
Changes a function makes outside itself, like editing a shared variable or writing to the console.
Reads text and turns it into a whole number. '42' becomes 42. A second value can set the number base.
The number base used to read digits. Radix 10 is normal counting; radix 2 is binary.
Short for "Not a Number". It is the result when a math step can't make a real number, like reading 'cat' as a number.

lessons.title: What is this? call, apply and bind
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, locate the best function implementation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Inside a regular function, `this` is a hidden value. It points at the object the function is working for right now. The rule: `this` is set by **how a function is called**, not where it was written. So one function can get a different `this` on each call.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: The word "me" on a name badge. Whoever wears the badge right now is "me". Hand the badge to someone else and "me" changes. Where it stops: an arrow function has no badge. It uses the `this` of the code around it.

cards.title: Step 1: a method call
cards.body: `hi` is a **method**: a function stored on an object. In `ann.hi()`, the object before the dot is `ann`. So inside `hi`, `this` is `ann`, and `this.name` is `'Ann'`.

cards.title: The rules, in order
items: `obj.fn()`: `obj`, the object before the dot
Plain call `fn()`, no dot: `undefined` in **strict mode** (stricter rules, set by `'use strict'` and always on in classes and modules). In sloppy mode, the **global object**
`new Fn()`: the object `new` just built
`call()`, `apply()` or `bind()`: whatever you pass first
Arrow function: no own `this`; it uses the outer one

cards.title: The lost method
cards.body: Copy a **method** out of its object and the dot is gone. In strict mode, `this` is then `undefined`, so `this.ticks` throws `TypeError`. Class bodies are always strict, so a copied class method fails the same way.

cards.title: call and apply: run it now
cards.body: `call()` runs the function now. Its first value becomes `this`, and the rest are passed one by one. `apply()` does the same, but takes the rest in one array. Both give `'Hi, Ann!'` here.

cards.title: bind: lock it for later
cards.code:
const hiAnn = intro.bind(ann, 'Hi'); // intro, ann from above
hiAnn('?');                          // 'Hi, Ann?'
hiAnn.call({ name: 'Bo' }, '?');     // still 'Hi, Ann?'
cards.body: `bind()` runs nothing. It returns a **bound function** with `this` and any first values locked in. Even `call()` can't change that `this`, as the last line shows. Only `new` ignores it. Arrows ignore all three: their `this` never changes.

Arrows as object methods. In `{ name: 'Ann', hi: () => this.name }`, the arrow does not read `name` from the object. It takes `this` from outside the object literal. Write a regular method: `hi() { return this.name; }`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Look left of the dot."** The object before the dot at call time is `this`. No dot: `undefined` in strict code. Arrows: look outside.

terms.say: A hidden value inside a regular function. It points at the object the function was called on, and it is set fresh on every call.
A function stored as a property of an object. You call it with a dot, like cart.total().
A safer mode of JavaScript, turned on with 'use strict', in classes and in modules. Silent mistakes become errors.
A line at the top of a file or function that switches on strict mode.
The big object that holds global things. In a browser it is window. In strict code a plain call doesn't use it as this.
Normal, non-strict JavaScript. It forgives some mistakes quietly instead of throwing errors.
A keyword that builds a fresh object from a function or a class. Inside that function, this is the fresh object.
The error you get when a value is the wrong kind for what you do, like reading a property of undefined.
A function method that runs the function right now, with this set to the first value and the other values passed one by one.
Like call(), but the values for the function are passed together in one array.
A function method that doesn't run anything. It returns a new function whose this is locked to the value you gave.
The new function bind() returns. Its this stays fixed, even if you try call() or apply() on it later.

lessons.title: Object literals, destructuring, getters
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, apply fundamentals of object implementation to solve the business requirement.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **object** is a bag of named values called **properties**. Each property has a **key** (its name) and a value. You build most objects with an **object literal**: curly braces holding `key: value` pairs. With `const user = { name: 'Ivy' }`, both `user.name` and `user['name']` give `'Ivy'`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A filing drawer with labeled folders. Each folder has a label (the key) and contents (the value). You can add, read or remove folders any time. Where it stops: labels are always strings or symbols. A number key like `1` is stored as the string `'1'`.

cards.title: Literal shortcuts
cards.body: Shorthand `size` reuses the variable's name as the key. A **computed key** in square brackets uses a value as the name: `[field]` becomes `color`. So `shirt['color']` is `'teal'`. Use **bracket notation** for keys held in a variable or keys like `'first-name'`.

cards.title: Destructuring an object
cards.body: **Destructuring** copies values out into variables in one line. `name: who` reads `name` and stores it in `who`. `plan = 'free'` is a default, used because `plan` is `undefined`. `...rest` collects what's left into a new object.

cards.title: Destructuring an array
cards.code:
const [first, , third] = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
// first = 'a', third = 'c'
cards.body: Arrays destructure by position, in square brackets. The empty slot between two commas skips `'b'`. So `first` is `'a'` and `third` is `'c'`.

cards.title: Getters and setters
cards.body: A **getter** (`get`) runs when you read a property. A **setter** (`set`) runs when you assign one. You use them like plain properties, with no parentheses. Reading gives `68`. Assigning `212` runs the setter, so `celsius` becomes `100`.

cards.title: Walking through an object
items: `Object.keys()`, `Object.values()`, `Object.entries()`: own **enumerable** (normal, listed) keys, values or `[key, value]` pairs, as arrays
`for...in`: walks keys, including ones **inherited** from a parent object
`for...of` needs an **iterable**, like an array. A plain object isn't one, so it throws `TypeError`
Own or inherited? `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (newer, ES2022) or `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)`

cards.body: Dot notation with a variable. With `const k = 'size'`, writing `obj.k` reads a property literally named "k". You get `undefined`. To use the variable's value as the key, write `obj[k]`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Dots for names you know, brackets for names you compute."**

A key written in square brackets inside an object literal. The value inside the brackets becomes the name.
Reading a property with square brackets, like obj[key]. It works with variables and odd names.
A short way to copy values out of an object or array into separate variables in one line.
A hidden function that runs when you read a property. It works out the value on the spot.
A hidden function that runs when you assign to a property. It decides what to do with the new value.
Gives an array of an object's own property names. For { a: 1, b: 2 } you get ['a', 'b'].
Gives an array of an object's own values. For { a: 1, b: 2 } you get [1, 2].
Gives an array of [name, value] pairs. For { a: 1 } you get [['a', 1]].
A setting on a property that says whether loops and Object.keys list it. Normal properties are enumerable.
A loop that visits an object's listed (enumerable) property names one by one, including ones it inherits.
A loop that visits the values of an array, string, Map or Set one by one. Plain objects don't work with it.
Something for...of can walk through one item at a time, like an array, a string, a Map or a Set.
Checks if an object holds a property itself, not borrowed from a parent. Gives true or false. Added in 2022.

lessons.title: Copying, comparing and freezing
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, apply fundamentals of object implementation to solve the business requirement.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A variable holding an object holds a **reference**: a pointer to the object, not a copy of it. Two variables can point at the same object. Change it through one, and the other sees the change.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A house address on a sticky note. Copy the note and both notes lead to one house. Paint the door through either note, and both see a red door. Where it stops: a **shallow copy** builds a new house, but the shed in the garden is still shared.

cards.title: Same object or not?
cards.body: `===` (strict equals) on objects checks **identity**: the same object, not the same contents. `c` is another name for `a`, so changing `c.x` changes `a.x`. `Object.is()` is like `===`, except `NaN` equals `NaN` and `0` differs from `-0`.

cards.title: Shallow copies share the inside
cards.body: Spread and `Object.assign()` copy only the top level. `copy.id` is its own value. But `copy.items` is the same array as `order.items`. So `push()`, which adds an item to the end, changes both.

cards.title: Deep copy options
items: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`: the classic copy for plain data. `JSON.stringify()` turns it into text, and `JSON.parse()` builds it back. It drops functions and `undefined`, and turns Dates into strings.
`structuredClone(obj)` (new in 2022): a real **deep copy** that keeps Dates, Maps and Sets. It throws `DataCloneError` on functions and DOM nodes.

cards.title: Locking an object
cards.body: `Object.freeze` blocks adding, removing and changing properties. `Object.seal` blocks adding and removing, but values can still change. `Object.preventExtensions` blocks only adding. In **strict mode**, a blocked change throws `TypeError`. In sloppy mode, it fails silently.

cards.title: Fine-grained control
cards.body: `Object.defineProperty()` adds one property with settings, like `Object.defineProperty(obj, 'id', { value: 7 })`. Any setting you leave out (`writable`, `enumerable`, `configurable`) defaults to `false`. So `id` can't change, is not **enumerable** (it won't show in `Object.keys`) and can't be deleted.

"Freezing makes it read-only all the way down." No: `Object.freeze` is shallow. A frozen object's nested objects can still change. And `const` only stops you reassigning the variable. It doesn't freeze the object at all.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Freeze: no add, no remove, no change. Seal: no add, no remove. Both: top layer only.**

terms.say: A pointer to an object. Copying a variable copies the pointer, so both point at the same object.
Strict equals. For objects it is true only when both sides are the very same object, not two look-alikes.
Whether two values are the very same object, not just objects that look alike.
Checks if two values are the same, like ===. But it says NaN equals NaN, and 0 is not the same as -0.
Short for "Not a Number". It is the odd value that is never === to itself.
A new object with the same top-level values. Anything nested inside is shared with the original.
Copies the properties of one object into another. Object.assign({}, a) makes a shallow copy of a.
Adds an item to the end of an array. ['pen'] with push('ink') becomes ['pen', 'ink'].
A copy where every nested object is copied too, so nothing is shared with the original.
Turns data into text in JSON format. { a: 1 } becomes the text {"a":1}.
Turns JSON text back into data. The text {"a":1} becomes the object { a: 1 }.
A newer built-in function (2022) that makes a deep copy. It can copy Dates, Maps and Sets, but not functions.
The error structuredClone throws when it meets something it can't copy, like a function.
Locks an object's top level. No properties can be added, removed or changed.
Locks an object's list of properties. You can't add or remove any, but you can still change values.
Stops new properties being added to an object. You can still change or delete the ones it has.
A safer mode of JavaScript. Here, a blocked change to a frozen object throws an error instead of failing quietly.
Adds or changes one property with exact settings, like whether it can be changed or listed.
A setting that decides whether a property shows up in loops like for...in and in Object.keys.

lessons.title: Prototypes and inheritance
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, apply fundamentals of object implementation to solve the business requirement.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every object has a hidden link to one other object, its **prototype**. Read a property the object doesn't have, and JavaScript follows the link and looks there. This is how many objects share one copy of a method, instead of each holding its own.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Asking around the family. You don't own a ladder, so you ask your parent, then your grandparent. The first one who has a ladder lends it. Where it stops: once you buy your own ladder, you use yours and never ask. That is **shadowing**.

cards.title: The prototype chain
cards.body: A prototype is an object too, so it has its own prototype, and so on. That line of links is the **prototype chain**. A read climbs it until it finds the property. The chain ends at `null` ("nothing here"). If no object on the way has the property, you get `undefined`.

cards.title: Object.create sets the link
cards.body: `Object.create(proto)` makes an empty object whose prototype is `proto`. `dog` has no `speak` of its own, so the call finds it on `animal`. `Object.getPrototypeOf()` reads the link. `Object.hasOwn()` gives `false`, because `speak` isn't stored on `dog` itself.

cards.title: Constructor functions
cards.body: A **constructor function** is a regular function meant for `new`. Methods put on its `prototype` property are shared by every **instance** (object it builds). So `c.honk()` finds `honk` there. `instanceof` checks whether `Car.prototype` is on the chain of `c`.

cards.title: What new Car('Kia') does
items: Creates an empty object
Links its prototype to `Car.prototype`
Runs `Car` with `this` set to that object
Returns it, unless `Car` returns an object of its own

cards.title: Reads climb, writes stay
cards.code:
dog.speak = () => 'woof'; // dog and animal from above
dog.speak();              // 'woof'
animal.speak();           // 'some sound'
cards.body: Reads walk the chain, but a plain assignment doesn't. `dog.speak = …` creates an own property on `dog`. It **shadows** the one on the prototype. `animal.speak` stays unchanged.

Mixing up `Car.prototype` with the prototype of `Car`. `Car.prototype` is what **instances** get. The prototype of `Car` itself is `Function.prototype`. Also, `__proto__` is an old way to reach the link; use `Object.getPrototypeOf`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Missing? Ask the parent."** Reads climb the chain until `null`. Own properties win. `instanceof` searches the chain for `Ctor.prototype`.

terms.say: A backup object linked to an object. If the object lacks a property, JavaScript looks in its prototype.
When an object has its own property with the same name as one on its prototype. Its own one wins.
The line of linked prototypes JavaScript walks, one by one, when looking up a property. It ends at null.
A value that means "nothing here, on purpose". The prototype chain stops when it reaches it.
The value you get when you read a property that no object on the chain has.
Makes a new, empty object and sets its prototype to the object you pass in.
Tells you which object is the prototype of the object you pass in.
Checks if an object holds a property itself, not borrowed through its prototype. Gives true or false.
A regular function meant to be called with new. It fills in a fresh object through this.
A keyword that builds a fresh object from a function or a class and links it to that function's prototype property.
One object built from a constructor or a class, like one cookie from a cookie cutter.
An operator that checks whether a constructor's prototype is somewhere on an object's prototype chain.
The shared prototype of every function. Methods like call and bind live there.
An old, built-in way to read or set an object's prototype. Modern code uses Object.getPrototypeOf instead.

lessons.title: Classes: extends, static and private
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, apply fundamentals of class implementation to solve the business requirement.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **class** is a blueprint for objects. It bundles a **constructor** (setup code that runs on `new`) with shared methods. Under the hood, classes are still functions and prototypes. So `typeof`, which names a value's kind, gives `'function'` for a class. The syntax is just cleaner and stricter.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A cookie cutter. The class is the cutter, and each cookie is an **instance**. A subclass is the same cutter with extra sprinkles. Where it stops: a `static` method belongs to the cutter itself, not to any cookie.

cards.title: A first class
cards.body: `new Cat('Tom')` builds an object and runs `constructor` with `this` set to it. So `this.name` becomes `'Tom'`. `speak` is stored once on the prototype and shared by every Cat **instance**.

cards.title: Static and private fields
cards.body: `#balance` is a **private field**: only code inside the class can reach it. `static count` lives on `Account` itself, not on instances. So `Account.count` is `1`, but `a.count` is `undefined`. Both features are ES2022.

cards.title: Inheritance with extends
cards.body: `extends` makes `Dog` a child class of `Animal`. A child constructor must call `super()`, which runs the parent's constructor, before it touches `this`. `super.speak()` calls the parent's version. Then `Dog` adds `' and barks'`.

cards.title: Class rules the exam loves
items: A class can't be used above its line: it has a **temporal dead zone** (a locked stretch), like `let`
Class bodies always run in **strict mode**
Calling a class without `new` throws `TypeError`
A subclass with no constructor passes all its values to the parent's
`static` members are used as `Account.count`, not through an instance

cards.title: Privacy before #
cards.body: Private `#` fields arrived in ES2022. Writing `obj.#balance` outside the class is a `SyntaxError`, found before any code runs. Older code hid data in **closures** (functions that keep private variables) or a `WeakMap`. The `_balance` naming habit hides nothing.

"Classes are hoisted like functions." They are hoisted, but locked until their line. `new Shape()` above `class Shape {}` throws `ReferenceError`. Touching `this` before `super()` in a subclass also throws `ReferenceError`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Super first, then this."** Static is on the class. Hash is private. A class is a function with stricter manners.

lessons.title: Modules: import and export
lessons.objective: Given a JavaScript module, give examples of how to use the module.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **module** is a file with its own private scope. Nothing inside leaks out unless you **export** it. Nothing comes in unless you **import** it. Each file does one job and says exactly what it shares.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Shops in a mall. Each shop keeps its stockroom private and puts some items in the window (exports). Other shops can order those items (imports). Where it stops: an import is a live window, not a copy. If the shop changes the item, you see the change.

cards.title: Named exports
cards.body: **Named exports** are imported by their exact names, in braces. `as` renames: in `app.js`, `PI` is called `pi`. `import * as math` gathers everything into one **namespace object**, so `math.area` and `math.PI` work too.

cards.title: The default export
cards.body: A module can have one **default export**. Import it with no braces, under any name you like: here `writeLog`. Default and named imports can share one line. (`console.log()` just prints the message.)

cards.title: How modules behave
items: Imports are **live bindings**: you see the exporter's updates, but assigning to an import throws `TypeError`
Imports are hoisted: imported files load and run before the module's own code
Modules always use **strict mode** and run only once, however many files import them

cards.title: Turning modules on
items: Browser: `<script type="module">`. It is deferred by default: it runs after the page's HTML is read
Node.js: `.mjs` files, or `"type": "module"` in `package.json` (the project's settings file)

cards.title: Load it only when needed
cards.body: `addEventListener()` runs the arrow on each click. **Dynamic import** with `import()` loads the module only then. It returns a **promise** (a value that arrives later) for the namespace object. `await` waits for it, inside an `async` function. `import()` works in classic scripts too.

"`export default const x = 1;` exports `x`." It's a `SyntaxError`. `export default` takes an expression, a function or a class, not `const`. Also: `import x from` gets the default, but `import { x } from` gets a named export.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Braces for names, no braces for the default."** One default per module, as many named exports as you like.

lessons.title: Scope, hoisting, the TDZ and closures
lessons.objective: Given a block of code, analyze the variable scope and the execution flow.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Scope** is where a variable can be seen. JavaScript looks up a name from the inside out: the current block, then the function, then the module or script, then the **global scope**. That path is the **scope chain**. Inner code can see outer variables. Outer code can't see inner ones.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Rooms with one-way windows. From the kitchen you can see the garden, but the garden can't see into the kitchen. Where it stops: `var` ignores small rooms (blocks). It only stops at function walls.

cards.title: var vs let
cards.body: `var` is **function-scoped**: it is visible in the whole function, so `console.log()` prints `1` for `a`. `let` and `const` are **block-scoped**: they live only inside their curly braces. So reading `b` outside them throws `ReferenceError`.

cards.title: Hoisting: var starts empty
cards.body: All declarations are **hoisted**: set up before the code runs. A `var` is set up holding `undefined`. So reading it above its line gives `undefined`, not an error. It gets `1` only when its line runs.

cards.title: The TDZ: let waits locked
cards.body: `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted too, but locked. The **temporal dead zone** (TDZ) runs from the start of the block to the declaration line. Touching the name there, even with `typeof`, throws `ReferenceError`. Once the line runs, the name works normally.

cards.title: Closures remember
cards.body: A **closure** is a function plus the variables from where it was made. The returned arrow keeps `count`, so `count` stays alive and private after `makeCounter` returns. `++count` adds one, then gives the new value: `1`, then `2`. Each call to `makeCounter` makes a fresh `count`.

cards.title: The loop trap
cards.body: `setTimeout()` runs each callback later, after the loop has finished. With `var` there is one `i` for the whole loop, so every callback reads its final value, `3`. `let` makes a new **binding** (a fresh `j`) for each round.
"`typeof` is always safe." Not in the TDZ. `typeof x` on a name that was never declared gives `'undefined'`. But on a `let x` declared later in the same scope, it throws `ReferenceError`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Var rises empty, let waits locked, closures pack a backpack."**

Prints a value to the console, the developer's text window. console.log(1) shows 1.

flashcards.front: Which kind of function can you call above the line where it is written?
flashcards.back: A **function declaration**. It is hoisted with its body. Function expressions and arrows wait for their variable: `var` gives `TypeError`, `let`/`const` give `ReferenceError`.

flashcards.front: What can't an arrow function do that a regular function can?
flashcards.back: Their own `this`, their own `arguments`, and the ability to be called with `new` (that throws `TypeError`). `this` comes from the surrounding code.

flashcards.front: How do you return an object literal from an arrow without `return`?
flashcards.back: Wrap it in parentheses: `() => ({ id: 1 })`. Without them, the braces are read as a function body and it returns `undefined`.

flashcards.front: When is a default parameter used?
flashcards.back: Only when the value is `undefined`, passed or missing. `null`, `0` and `''` are real values, so the default is skipped.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between rest and spread?
flashcards.back: Both use three dots. **Rest** in a parameter list gathers extra values into a real array. **Spread** in a call or a literal unpacks an array or object into separate values.

flashcards.front: What is the `arguments` object?
flashcards.back: A list-like object in regular functions holding every value passed in. It has `length` and numbered slots, but no array methods like `map`. Arrow functions don't have their own.

flashcards.front: What is a callback?
flashcards.back: A function you pass to another function so it can call it, now (like `map`) or later (like `setTimeout`).

flashcards.front: Why does `['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)` give `[1, NaN, NaN]`?
flashcards.back: `map` passes the index as the second value. `parseInt` reads it as the radix. Use `map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))` or `map(Number)`.

flashcards.front: What is a higher-order function?
flashcards.back: A function that takes a function as a value or returns one. Examples: `map`, `filter`, or a factory like `multiplier(2)` that returns a new function.

flashcards.front: What decides `this` in a regular function?
flashcards.back: How it is called. `obj.fn()` gives `obj`. A plain `fn()` gives `undefined` in strict mode. `new` gives the new object. `call`, `apply` and `bind` set it directly.

flashcards.front: How do `call()`, `apply()` and `bind()` differ?
flashcards.back: `call()` runs now, values one by one. `apply()` runs now, values in an array. `bind()` returns a new function with `this` fixed.

flashcards.front: Can `call()` change the `this` of a bound function or an arrow?
flashcards.back: No. A bound function keeps its bound `this`, and an arrow always uses the outer `this`. Only `new` overrides a bound `this`.

flashcards.front: How do you read a property whose name is in a variable?
flashcards.back: Use bracket notation: `obj[key]`. `obj.key` looks for a property literally named "key".

flashcards.front: How do you rename a value and give it a backup while destructuring?
flashcards.back: `const { name: who = 'guest' } = user;` reads `name`, stores it in `who`, and uses `'guest'` if it is `undefined`.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?
flashcards.back: `for...in` loops over property names, inherited ones included. `for...of` loops over the values of something you can step through, like an array. A plain object doesn't work with `for...of`.

flashcards.front: Does `{ ...obj }` make a deep copy?
flashcards.back: No, a shallow one. Top-level values are copied, but nested objects are shared. For a deep copy of plain data use `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`; newer code can use `structuredClone(obj)`.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `Object.freeze` and `Object.seal`?
flashcards.back: Freeze: no adding, removing or changing. Seal: no adding or removing, but values can change. Both are shallow.

flashcards.front: Why is `{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }` false?
flashcards.back: `===` on objects asks "is it the very same object?" These are two different objects, even with the same contents.

flashcards.front: Where does JavaScript look when an object doesn't have a property?
flashcards.back: Up the prototype chain: the object's prototype, then that one's prototype, and so on. The chain ends at `null`. If nobody has it, you get `undefined`.

flashcards.front: What does `x instanceof C` check?
flashcards.back: Whether `C.prototype` is somewhere on the prototype chain of `x`. For an object made with `new C()`, it is `true`.

flashcards.front: What does `Object.create(proto)` do?
flashcards.back: It makes a new empty object whose prototype is `proto`. Use `Object.create(null)` for an object with no prototype at all.

flashcards.front: What must a subclass constructor do before using `this`?
flashcards.back: Call `super()`. Touching `this` first throws `ReferenceError`.

flashcards.front: Where does a `static` method live?
flashcards.back: On the class itself. Call it as `ClassName.method()`, not through an instance.

flashcards.front: Can you use a class above its declaration?
flashcards.back: No. Class declarations are in the temporal dead zone until their line, so early use throws `ReferenceError`.

flashcards.front: How do you import a default export and a named export together?
flashcards.back: `import main, { helper } from './file.js';` The default has no braces and any name; named ones use braces.

flashcards.front: Can you reassign an imported variable?
flashcards.back: No. Imports are read-only, so assigning throws `TypeError`. But they stay connected (live bindings): you do see changes the exporting module makes.

flashcards.front: What does dynamic `import()` return?
flashcards.back: A promise for an object holding all the module's exports (the namespace object). Use it to load code only when needed. It works in classic scripts too.

flashcards.front: What is the temporal dead zone?
flashcards.back: The part of a scope before a `let`, `const` or `class` line. Touching the name there throws `ReferenceError`.

flashcards.front: What is a closure?
flashcards.back: A function plus the variables from where it was made. It keeps them alive after the outer function returns, like a counter that remembers its `count`.

flashcards.front: Why does a `var` loop with `setTimeout` log the last value every time?
flashcards.back: `var` makes one shared variable for the loop. The callbacks run later and all read its final value. `let` makes a new binding each round.

flashcards.front: Is `var` block-scoped?
flashcards.back: No. `var` is function-scoped, so it is visible in the whole function. `let` and `const` are block-scoped.
